Summary of Remarks
With respect to the rejected claims, the cited art fails to disclose or suggest a wearable fetal health monitoring device configured for continuous non-invasive non- clinical monitoring and having a microcontroller configured for:
monitoring fetal movement (fM) using the passive sensor while
operating in a first mode, wherein the first mode is a reduced power
mode; and
upon detecting reduced fMV activity, transitioning to a second mode

determining fetal heart rate variability (fHRV) data from the mechano-acoustically sensed fPCG data; and
providing an alert to the expecting mother based on the fHRV data.
Status of the Claims
Claims 1-14 and 16-21 were previously pending. Claims 1, 3-9, 11, 13-14, 17, and 19-21 are amended herein. Claim 15 was previously canceled. Claims 2, 10, 12, and 18 are canceled herein. Claims 22-25 are added herein. As such, claims 1, 3-9, 11, 13-14, 17, and 19-25 remain pending.


Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112

0.432.067Claim 1, 12, 17, and 21 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The Office Action contends the subject matter was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to a person of ordinary skill in the art had possession of the claimed invention.
Regarding claims 1, 17, and 21 the Office Action further identifies the limitation reciting "identify a noise correction value" based on comparing "the first mHR value with the second mHR value."
Claims 1, 17, and 21 have been amended to remove the above limitation.
Regarding claims 1, 17, and 21 the Office Action contends the limitation of "a ferroelectric nanogenerator sensor that detects abdominal pressure waves" seems unclear.
Claims 1, 17, and 21 have been amended to remove the above limitation.
Regarding claim 12, the Office Action further identifies the limitation reciting "deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal" based on "using at least one of the first mHR value and the second mHR value."
Claim 12 has been canceled rendering its rejection moot.
Accordingly, it is respectfully submitted that the rejection of claims 1, 17, and 21 under 35 USC § 112 be withdrawn.

Claim Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. 101

Claims 1-20 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. The Office Action further contends claims 1-20 are directed toward an abstract idea related to certain methods of organizing human activity such as commercial or legal interactions including advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, or business relations and fail to pass Step 2A - Prong 1 of the Alice/Mayo analysis. Additionally, the Office Action contends claims 1-20 are not integrated into a practical application and fail to pass Step 2A - Prong 2 of the Alice/Mayo analysis. Finally, the Office Action contends claims 1-20 do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception and fail to pass Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis.
A clean version of amended claim 1 is recited as follows:
A wearable fetal health monitoring device for determining a health

fetus, the wearable fetal health monitoring device comprising:
a passive sensor configured to provide mechano-acoustically
sensed phonocardiogram (aPCG) data from a first location on a maternal
torso;
an optical sensor configured to provide optically sensed maternal
photoplethysmogram (mPPG) data from a second location on the
maternal torso;

the fHRV data.
The following remarks will address claims 1-20 in regard to Step 2A - Prong 2 and Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis.

"For example, if the additional limitations reflect an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to another technology or technical field, the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application and thus imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception.

Amended claim 1 recites additional limitations that reflect an improvement of a technical field (e.g., determining a heath condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus). As such, determining a heath condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus is improved.
A person of ordinary skill in the art would understand that such a method must be implemented on a computing device. Accordingly, amended claim 1 recites a practical application. As such for the reasons above, amended claim 1 passes Step 2A Prong Two of the Alice/Mayo analysis.

Eligibility Decision (Berkheimer v. HP, Inc.)" (Apr. 19, 2018),
The above USPTO Memorandum recites in Section III updated requirements for a Step 2B analysis of Alice/Mayo. As Applicant understands this guidance, the Examiner must support a 101 rejection using at least one of the following four points of the Memorandum to determine that the combination of elements are well-understood, routine or conventional in nature:
1. A citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement
made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the well- understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
A   specification  demonstrates  the  well-understood,  routine, conventional nature of additional elements when it describes the additional elements as well-understood or routine or conventional (or an equivalent term), as a commercially available product, or in a manner that indicates that the additional elements are sufficiently well-known that the specification does not need to describe the particulars of such additional elements to satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). A finding that an element is well-understood, routine, or conventional cannot be based only on the fact that the specification is silent with
respect to describing such element.
2. A citation to one or more of the court decisions discussed in MPEP Q
2106.05(d)(II) as noting the well-understood, routine, conventional
nature of the additional element(s).

SVG
{EMBED HERE}
0.432.0673. A citation to a publication that demonstrates the well-understood,
routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s). An appropriate publication could include a book, manual, review article, or other source that describes the state of the art and discusses what is well-known and in common use in the relevant industry. It does not include all items that might otherwise qualify as a "printed publication" as used in 35 U.S.C. § 102.3. Whether something is disclosed in a document that is considered a "printed publication"
under 3 5 U.S. C § 102 is a distinct inquiry from whether something is well-known, routine, conventional activity. A document may be a printed publication but still fail to establish that something it describes is well-understood, routine, conventional activity. See Exergen Corp., 2018 WL 1193529, at *4 (the single copy of a thesis written in German and located in a German university library considered to be a "printed publication" in Hall "would not suffice to establish that something is 'well-understood, routine, and conventional activity previously engaged in by scientists who work in the field"'). The nature of the publication and the description of the additional elements in the publication would need to demonstrate that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field, comparable to the types of activity or elements that are so well-known that they do not need to be described in detail in a patent application to satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). For example, while U.S. patents and published applications are publications, merely finding the additional element in a single patent or published application would not be sufficient to demonstrate that the additional element is well- understood, routine, conventional, unless the patent or published
SVG
{EMBED HERE}
0.432.067application demonstrates that the additional element are widely
prevalent or in common use in the relevant field.
4. A statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well- understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
This option should be used only when the examiner is certain, based upon his or her personal knowledge, that the additional element(s) represents well-understood, routine, conventional activity engaged in by those in the relevant art, in that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field, comparable to the types of activity or elements that are so well-known that they do not need to be described in detail in a patent application to satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). Procedures for taking official notice and addressing an applicant's challenge to official notice are discussed in MPEP Q
2144.03.
Taking into account the above guidance, it is clear that the additional elements recited in the present claims amount to significantly more than the judicial exception and therefor are patent-eligible subject matter because the additional elements is not well- understood, routine, or conventional in nature as required by at least one of the above four points of the Memorandum.
Regarding point 1 of the Memorandum, nowhere has Applicant cited in the Specification, or during prosecution that the above additional elements would be well- understood, routine, or conventional in nature to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the priority date of the application.
Regarding point 2 of the Memorandum, Applicant is unaware of any court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d)(II) as noting a well-understood, routine, or conventional in nature the above additional elements.

SVG
{EMBED HERE}
0.432.067Regarding point 3 of the Memorandum, the Office Action fails to cite any references that disclose the above additional elements as well-understood, routine, or conventional in nature.
Regarding point 4 of the Memorandum, the Examiner has not taken official notice in the Office Action that the above additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional in nature.
As such, amended claim 1 in addition to passing Step 2A also passes Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis.
Claims 2, 10, 12, and 18 has been cancelled rendering their rejection moot.
Claims 3-9, 11, 13-14, and 16 depend directly from amended claim 1 and are allowable at least by virtue of its dependence from amended claim 1.
Claim 17 and 21 have been amended to include features that are similar to amended claim 1. As such claims 17 and 21 are also allowable.
Claims 19-20 depend directly for amended claim 17 and are allowable at least by virtue of their dependence from amended claim 17.
Accordingly, it is respectfully submitted that the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 of claims 1, 3-9, 11, 13-14, 17, and 19-21 be withdrawn.
